_about: Build review of every counterexample confirmed by the second model (first against one Nemotron 3 Super run, then against most of five), done by reading the policy text during development (2026-10-28). verdict: upheld (the policy as written says this), qualified (true as written, with a caveat a reader needs), rejected (the policy says otherwise; both models missed it). 'match' picks the finding by a phrase from its summary.

reviews.note: Charity is limited to uninsured or underinsured patients; Colorado HDC must screen an insured patient who asks.
The policy requires the date of service to be within 181 days of applying, with no extra window after an insurance adjustment.
181 days from service can end before 240 days after the first bill when insurance delays the bill.
ECAs no sooner than 120 days after the first statement; statements may start on day 46.
ECAs not until at least 120 days after the first post-discharge statement; no 182-day floor stated.
Assistance is for people who are uninsured or underinsured.
Charity care is for qualified patients who are uninsured or underinsured.
Residency within an Intermountain service area is required for non-emergent services.
Eligibility is considered for uninsured or underinsured individuals.
Applications are due within 45 days of service (or 45 days after an insurance payment or Medicaid denial); Colorado allows at least 181 days.
The policy also allows 45 days from the date of primary insurance payment, which meets Colorado's insured-patient window. Both models missed that option.
Payment plans must be at least $25 a month; for very low incomes that exceeds 4% of monthly income. Accounts must also be paid within 24 months.
This is a plain-language summary; it also offers help 'if it would be a financial hardship to pay', which may cover insured patients.
The sliding scale stops at 200%, but the policy says discounts 'could include the HDC program' without describing it.
Income-based assistance requires the patient to be uninsured or under-insured (out-of-pocket costs exceed ability to pay).
A band gap: 100% at 250% or less, discounts 'between 251% and 400%'. Likely a rounding convention.

The clause is 'The patient received a service at AVRMC or an AVRMC physician clinic', which is about where care happened, not where the patient lives. Both models encoded it as a service-area residency rule.
The policy covers 'an insured patient that has specifically requested screening', as Colorado law requires. Both models dropped that part.

Banner's document is a summary of its programs: uninsured up to 400%, underinsured, and medically indigent (medical bills over a share of income). An insured patient with a smaller bill fits none of them as written; the full policy may say more.
Charity is considered for individuals who are uninsured, underinsured and ineligible for government programs; HDC must screen an insured patient who asks.
'Ineligible for any government health care program' was encoded as 'has not applied for Medicaid', which the policy doesn't say.
Same wording: charity for individuals who are uninsured, underinsured and ineligible for government programs.
'Ineligible for any government health care program' was encoded as 'has not applied for Medicaid', which the policy doesn't say.
Applications must be in 'prior to 180 days from the date of the initial account statement'; 501(r) requires accepting them for 240 days.
Assistance is considered for individuals who are uninsured or underinsured and unable to pay.
A band gap: the sliding scale's bands end at 200% and restart at 201%. Likely a rounding convention.
A band gap: bands end at 100% and restart at 101%. Likely a rounding convention.
HDC and CICP are described as 'discounted care programs for patients who are Uninsured or Underinsured'; Colorado law has the hospital screen an insured patient who asks.
'Unable to pay for their care' isn't a fact the audit can express; the model forced it onto another variable, so this case is an artifact.
'Unable to pay for their care' isn't a fact the audit can express; the model forced it onto another variable, so this case is an artifact.
'Unable to pay for those services' isn't a fact the audit can express; the model forced it onto another variable, so this case is an artifact.

reviews.match: meets every requirement, but no rule
reviews.note: A band gap: the policy's bands stop at 200% and restart at 201% (and at 225%/226%). Likely a rounding convention, not an intended exclusion.

The policy requires other payment options, including public programs, to be exhausted 'unless prohibited by local, state, or federal laws'. Colorado prohibits denying discounted care because a patient hasn't applied for public benefits, so the policy's own exception should cover this; it just doesn't say so.
The policy describes assistance for patients who are uninsured or underinsured; HDC must screen an insured patient who asks.
A band gap: full charity for '0 - 250%' of the poverty level, an expanded policy for 'between 251 and 400 percent'. Likely a rounding convention.
